A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TheoryCoder under the same title and authors. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendix A are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original TheoryCoder evaluations on grid-world games, including API usage, task success, planning-time ablations, and model-transfer results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, behavioral analyses, failure cases, and a custom-game experiment.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 removes v1's model-predicted next-state assignment from the environment-execution loop before storing actual transitions. This is a limited pseudocode correction; both versions already describe collecting real environment transitions. The hierarchical planning architecture, synthesis/refinement procedure, and Appendix A prompts remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Sections 4.7–4.8 add two KekeCompetition levels requiring sacrifice of controlled characters and a ten-level custom box-clustering game with lethal cherries. These introduce distinct task requirements. Baba is AI coverage remains reported in Section 4.2 despite removal of its dedicated transfer section.

E2.justification: v2 adds EMPA to the reported VGDL comparison in Table 3, a fully specified PDDL/Fast Downward baseline to the runtime comparison in Table 4, and WorldCoder to the BabyAI/Minigrid comparison in Table 7. v1 primarily compares against GPT-o1 and TheoryCoder's own ablation.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce environment-step and learning-efficiency metrics, token accounting, a 500-environment-step budget, and a matched WorldCoder curriculum with MCTS depth 30 and 50 API calls per level. A failure case is tested through 25 calls. The original six-call benchmark allowance and 500-second planning timeout remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds gameplay heatmaps for KekeCompetition levels 11 and 13, initialization-failure observations, two challenging failure cases, and a custom-game test addressing possible training-data contamination. These substantially extend diagnosis beyond v1's planning and prompting ablations. The dedicated transfer illustration is removed, although its broad outcome remains mentioned.

E5.justification: Section 4.7 newly discloses qualitatively that repeated runs sometimes become stuck. It supplies no run count, seeds, failure frequency, or uncertainty estimates. Runtime averaging over five runs was already reported in v1 and is retained; an increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds EMPA step/success results, FD runtimes, and WorldCoder comparisons: Table 7 reports 69,402 tokens and 100% success for TheoryCoder versus 388,861 and 83% for WorldCoder. Figure 15 adds four API calls across ten custom-game levels; Section 4.7 reports two failures, one after 25 calls. Original API-call totals persist; reversed Sokoban level/runtime ordering does not establish a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: The classical-planning formulation, abstraction definitions, and Equations 1–4 retain their mathematical substance. The added learning-efficiency formula is an adopted evaluation metric credited to prior work, not a new theoretical development. No proofs or formal guarantees are added.

C1.justification: The abstract and central introductory/concluding claims remain the same: combining Python world-model synthesis with hierarchical abstractions improves planning and learning efficiency. The conclusion retains the 24.5-fold API-usage reduction claim. New experiments expand support without redefining these main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of initialization traps, overgeneralization of death-avoidance rules, and differences between object-oriented exploration and GPT-o1's repetitive behavior. It proposes maintaining alternative world models. Demonstrated transfer across visually distinct games in v1 becomes a future-work possibility in Section 4.5, although Section 4.2 still retains the Baba is AI success statement.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new WorldCoder comparison's MCTS depth, request cap, and curriculum matching, and specifies that the full-PDDL baseline is manually constructed without learning or revision. Existing API settings, the code-access link, and Appendix A's initialization and revision prompts remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion concerning Guzdial et al.'s game-engine learning, Ruoss et al.'s LMAct benchmark, Minigrid, and Sutton et al.'s temporal abstraction framework. The principal positioning within theory-based RL, program synthesis, and bilevel planning remains intact.

P1.justification: Related work gains numbered subsections, while the introduction and method exposition are shortened by removing travel and household examples and repetitive PDDL explanations. New experimental subsections are integrated, and publication and author-role text changes. Most existing prose and the main section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with new comparison tables, an FD column in the runtime table, a learning-efficiency chart, gameplay heatmaps, failure illustrations, and custom-game screenshots/results. It also replaces the BabyAI screenshot and removes v1's transfer figure. These changes extend beyond renumbering and page reflow.

improvement.justification: v2 materially addresses v1's limited comparative validation through relevant WorldCoder and full-PDDL baselines, environment-step comparisons, a custom-game test, and concrete failure cases. These strengthen evidence for the contribution and clarify its limits. Sparse uncertainty reporting, conflicting transfer language, and an apparent Figure 6/Table 3 inconsistency remain: the Push Boulders efficiency bar is about 0.021, whereas the stated formula and table imply 4/236, about 0.017. Despite these weaknesses, the stronger comparisons and explicit failure evidence provide a substantial net improvement.
